Just to jog your memory, a tayuu was the Kyoto equivalent of the Tokyo (Edo) oiran. She was the highest class of courtesan, whose arts included music, dancing and chanoyu (tea ceremony) like a geiko, but also sex. As geiko and geisha became more popular, they became the epitome of iki (chic). The splendour of the tayuu became seen as flippant and wasteful in wartime Japan, and with the prohibition of prostitution in 1958, oiran and tayuu culture was almost completely wiped out.

Tayuu and oiran who still operate now do so as part of Japanese historic revival. The Yoshiwara oiran-dochu occurs in Asakusa on the second Saturday of April.

According to Oiran-Geisha, there are six tayuu working in Kyoto. I know of Tsukasa-tayuu, her daughter Aoi-tayuu (formerly known as Furisode-tayuu when she was an apprentice), Kisaragi-tayuu, Sakaragi-tayuu (unsure if still active), and Kikugawa-tayuu. That leaves one I don't know of.
